title: Five C/V stage graphs on four schedules each
formula: alternating matmul and vector stages over the pattern string, FP16 operands, FP32 accumulation, FP16 between stages, 32-row tiles
study_for: A controlled comparison, which is what makes it teachable: the four schedules of one graph compute the same function, so if `pipeline` disagrees with `serial` the schedule is the only thing that can have caused it. Start with CVC, read `cvc_serial` and `cvc_pipeline` side by side, then look at what `resident` adds on top.

Every kernel is written out in full instead of being built by a Python loop over stages. That is deliberate: a stage delay, a slot index and an edge's owner are visible in the source of the kernel that has them, and nothing is decided at device-loop time. Twenty near-identical kernels is the price of being able to diff two of them.

Sizes are chosen against the slot ring, not for coverage: 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 tiles make it wrap zero, once and several times. A schedule bug that needs a wrap is invisible at one tile and obvious at seven.

`pipeline` is the only schedule that also runs on two cores, at the three sizes where the ring wraps. It is the schedule whose correctness depends on how items are split across cores, so that is where the split and the delay can interact.

The per-tile mark in column 0 of `x`. A lost drain, a wrong delayed index and a stale resident slot all move rows between tiles; without the mark those show up as a plausible number, with it they show up as the wrong tile's value.
do_not_copy_when: Your row count is not a multiple of 32. There is no tail handling anywhere in this folder — the tail is left out so the scheduling question stands alone.
You want a tuned kernel. These are correctness demonstrations of scheduling shapes; nothing here is measured, and `resident` is not automatically faster than `serial` at these sizes.

You need more than three weights or a graph that is not a simple alternation. The pattern string is walked stage by stage against w0, w1, w2 — a branch or a shared stage is outside what these twenty kernels express.
